qt: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE) Subject:

High temperatures, drought and extreme weather events are changing production conditions for some of Europe’s best-known traditional products, from alpine cheeses to champagne. This state of affairs is particularly relevant for geographical indication (GI) products, as they have to comply with strict provisions linking their characteristics and specific production methods to a given territory. In 2026, Abondance cheese producers had to use the hay they were storing for winter early because droughts in Haute-Savoie reduced the amount of available pastureland. Six other PDO cheeses have been granted temporary derogations by the French authorities. These climate-related pressures aren’t confined to one Member State. In Spain, the rules for Antequera PDO olive oil have been amended to address the impact of drought, while Italy has granted derogations to certain PDO cheeses concerning the proportion of dried fodder in cattle feed. In the wine sector, the grape harvest keeps being brought forward because of high temperatures. In the Champagne region, a combination of drought, warm February weather and spring frosts have prompted requests for a derogation temporarily allowing an alcohol content of up to 15 % for finished products, up from the traditional ceiling of 13 %. How will the Commission adapt the regulation governing geographical indications to the reality of climate change?
